title: Housing Discrimination Lawsuit - The Foundation of Racism
synopsis: In 1973, the Department of Justice sued Donald Trump and his father Fred Trump for systematically discriminating against Black renters across their housing empire. Federal investigators found that Trump Management marked rental applications from Black applicants with a C for colored and routinely told Black prospective tenants that no apartments were available, while immediately showing units to white applicants.
supported_event_claim: The Justice Department sued Trump Management in 1973 over alleged racial discrimination in rental housing; Donald and Fred Trump settled in 1975 without admitting wrongdoing under terms requiring anti-discrimination measures.

sources.title: Inside the government’s racial bias case against Donald Trump’s company, and how he fought it
FBI releases file on 1970s Trump housing discrimination case

research_reason: Contemporaneous government case details and later reporting support the lawsuit and settlement. The coded application evidence is described in government interview accounts; the settlement was not an admission.

title: Central Park Five Death Penalty Ad - Calling for Blood

supported_event_claim: After the Central Park jogger assault, Trump bought full-page ads in four New York newspapers urging reinstatement of the death penalty.

sources.title: DEADLY DONALD

research_reason: UPI’s contemporaneous report directly describes the ads. The supplied synopsis’s precise $85,000 amount is not established by this source.

title: Birtherism Conspiracy - The Big Lie Prototype

supported_event_claim: Trump promoted doubts about Barack Obama’s birthplace for years and acknowledged in September 2016 that Obama was born in the United States.

sources.title: Trump admits Obama was born in U.S., but falsely blames Clinton for starting rumors

research_reason: The report documents the long-running claims and the 2016 reversal. It supports the conduct but does not itself establish the entry’s broad causal description of Trump’s political career.

title: Classified Documents at Mar-a-Lago - National Security Theft

supported_event_claim: The federal indictment alleged that after leaving office Trump retained hundreds of classified documents at Mar-a-Lago, including documents concerning nuclear programs and defense capabilities, without authorization.

sources.title: Superseding indictment, United States v. Trump, Nauta, and De Oliveira
Trump classified documents at Mar-a-Lago

research_reason: The indictment directly supports the alleged retention and its contents. These are allegations in a charging document; the entry’s characterization as established theft is not adopted here.

sources.title: Administration of Donald J. Trump, 2017: Executive Order 13769 description
sources.publisher: Office of the Federal Register, National Archives and Records Administration

title: Miss Universe Pageant Voyeurism - 'I Can Do Whatever I Want'
synopsis: As owner of the Miss Universe, Miss USA, and Miss Teen USA pageants, Donald Trump routinely exploited his position to engage in predatory behavior toward contestants, including walking into dressing rooms while women and teenage girls were changing...
supported_event_claim: Former pageant contestants reported that Trump entered contestants’ dressing areas while they were changing; Trump also described entering backstage areas in a 2005 interview.

sources.title: Miss USA Contestant: Donald Trump Walked in on Naked Women in Dressing Room
The allegations about Donald Trump and Miss Teen USA contestants

research_reason: The sources distinguish contestants’ allegations from Trump’s recorded account. The packet’s characterization of routine predatory conduct and the full 1996–2016 span are broader than these sources establish.

Trump criticized for dining with far-right activist Nick Fuentes and rapper Ye

title: Housing Discrimination Lawsuit

sources.title: Inside the government’s racial bias case against Donald Trump’s company, and how he fought it
FBI releases file on 1970s Trump housing discrimination case

research_reason: Credible reporting documents the case and settlement. The packet’s placeholder DOJ and settlement links are not sources, and no tenant testimony records were linked in the packet.

title: Kung Flu Racist Term
synopsis: Trump repeatedly used racist term Kung Flu for COVID-19, fueling anti-Asian hate crimes during pandemic.
supported_event_claim: Trump used ‘kung flu’ to refer to COVID-19 at public events in June 2020; the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights documents concerns that racialized pandemic terminology could stigmatize Asian communities.

sources.title: Trump again uses racially insensitive term to describe coronavirus
The Federal Response to Anti-Asian Racism in the United States

research_reason: Sources establish the phrase and documented concern about stigmatizing effects, but do not establish that this phrase caused particular hate crimes or quantify its effect.

title: Twitter Covfefe Mystery
synopsis: Trump posted incomprehensible tweet covfefe at midnight, left it up for hours, sparked global confusion and memes.
supported_event_claim: Trump posted ‘Despite the constant negative press covfefe’ shortly after midnight on May 31, 2017; the post was deleted several hours later and he joked about its meaning in a follow-up tweet.

sources.title: Tweets of May 31, 2017
sources.publisher: The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara

sources.title: Trump targets ‘negative press covfefe’ in garbled midnight tweet that becomes worldwide joke

research_reason: The American Presidency Project archives the tweets and timestamps; The Washington Post reports the deletion and reaction. The record’s claim that the meaning was never clarified is not necessary to establish the event.

title: Staring at Solar Eclipse
synopsis: Trump looked directly at solar eclipse without protective glasses despite widespread warnings about eye damage.
supported_event_claim: Trump was photographed briefly looking toward the partially eclipsed sun without protective eyewear while viewing the 2017 eclipse; NASA warned that looking directly at the sun can damage vision.

sources.title: Trump watches eclipse from White House
NASA Recommends Safety Tips to View the August Solar Eclipse

research_reason: CBS/AP reports the brief glance and that Trump wore glasses for most of the viewing; NASA provides the safety guidance. The packet overstates the duration as sustained looking.

title: Porn Star Hush Money
synopsis: Trump paid $130,000 hush money to porn star Stormy Daniels to hide affair during 2016 election campaign.
supported_event_claim: Michael Cohen wired approximately $130,000 to Stormy Daniels’s attorney on October 27, 2016, as part of an agreement to suppress her story before the election; Cohen later pleaded guilty to campaign-finance violations related to the payment.

sources.title: Michael Cohen Pleads Guilty in Manhattan Federal Court to Eight Counts, Including Criminal Tax Evasion and Campaign Finance Violations
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Southern District of New York

sources.title: Trump hush money trial: A timeline of key events in the case

research_reason: The DOJ record and AP timeline support the transfer and its context. It was Cohen who wired the money; the entry’s claim that Trump personally paid it on October 27 is not supported by these sources.

title: Bleach Injection COVID Cure
synopsis: Trump suggested injecting bleach and disinfectant as COVID treatment during live press briefing, causing poison control spike.
supported_event_claim: During an April 23, 2020 briefing, Trump speculated about whether disinfectant could be applied by injection or ‘almost a cleaning’ and asked whether light could be brought inside the body as a COVID-19 treatment.

sources.title: April 23, 2020: Task Force Briefing on the Coronavirus Pandemic
The White House Spins Trump’s Disinfectant Remarks

research_reason: The transcript and fact check support the remarks. The packet’s ‘injecting bleach’ phrasing is not a precise quotation, and the asserted nationwide poison-control spike is not supported by these sources.

title: Mocking Disabled Reporter Kovaleski
synopsis: Trump physically mocked disabled reporter Serge Kovaleski, imitating his congenital joint condition at rally.
supported_event_claim: At a November 2015 rally, Trump made gestures while discussing New York Times reporter Serge Kovaleski, who has arthrogryposis; contemporaneous video and reporting documented the episode and Kovaleski’s response.

sources.title: Trump draws scornful rebuke for mocking reporter with disability
Trump mocks disabled reporter

research_reason: The report and video establish the event. The record’s paraphrase of the movement as a physical imitation is supported by contemporaneous coverage, without inferring motive beyond the documented exchange.

Tweets of February 15, 2017
sources.publisher: The American Presidency Project, UC Santa Barbara

research_reason: ABC News reports the exact February 17 statement, and the archival tweet collection documents repeated ‘fake news’ language. These sources do not establish the entry’s broader causal claims about danger to journalists or democracy.

sources.title: April 23, 2020: Task Force Briefing on the Coronavirus Pandemic

title: Toilet Paper Shoe Air Force One
synopsis: Trump walked up Air Force One stairs with toilet paper stuck to his shoe, completely unaware for several minutes.
supported_event_claim: On October 4, 2018, video showed paper, described as toilet paper or possibly a napkin, attached to Trump’s shoe as he boarded Air Force One.

sources.title: Trump boards Air Force One with toilet paper in tow. (Or was it a napkin?)
Donald Trump boards Air Force One with paper stuck to his shoe – video

research_reason: The Washington Post and Guardian report the visible paper and provide video-based coverage. Sources do not establish that he was unaware for several minutes or that staff failed to notice.

title: Autopen Document Signing Robot
synopsis: Trump used autopen signing robot to forge his signature on official documents, including legislation.
supported_event_claim: No credible source located supports the packet’s claim that Trump used an autopen to forge his signature on official documents or legislation throughout 2017–2021.
research_reason: Targeted searches surfaced reporting that autopen use by presidents can be lawful and that Trump later acknowledged limited autopen use for unimportant papers, but no evidence supporting this specific historical allegation. Available sources contradict the implication that autopen use is inherently forgery.

title: Windmill Vibrations Cause Cancer

supported_event_claim: At an April 2, 2019 Republican fundraiser, Trump said wind-turbine noise causes cancer; AP reported that this claim was not supported by evidence and cited the American Cancer Society’s lack of credible evidence linking windmill noise and cancer.

sources.title: AP FACT CHECK: Trump is tilting at wind farms again
Donald Trump’s ridiculous link between cancer, wind turbines

research_reason: Contemporaneous AP coverage and a fact check support the remark and assess the health claim. The source concerns turbine noise, not vibrations as phrased in the packet.
